method: Two-stage: one process wrote each article from sources it fetched and read; a separate process, which did not write it and was not asked to agree with it, then re-read every cited source itself and ruled on every numeric claim, quoted phrase, named study, date and attributed statement. The checker was instructed to fix what it found rather than report it, and to leave no claim standing that it could not verify. This is the first wave in which author and checker were different processes; earlier batches record honestly that they were not.

findings.claim: A litre of blood carries roughly 197 mL of oxygen protein-bound against about 3 mL dissolved at atmospheric tension
findings.note: "Hemoglobin carries 98% of the oxygen in the blood in the protein-bound form, approximately 197 ml/L"; "only 3ml O2/L of blood is dissolved at atmospheric oxygen tension."

findings.claim: A split usually quoted as 98 per cent to 2 per cent
findings.note: "Only 2% of oxygen in the bloodstream is dissolved directly in the plasma component of blood compared to 98% of oxygen in the protein-bound state to hemoglobin."

findings.claim: Quoted: "reveals a sigmoid curve"
findings.note: "Plotting oxygen tension (x) vs saturation (y) reveals a sigmoid curve..." Verbatim.

findings.claim: Quoted: "whereas that of other oxygen-carrying molecules (such as Myoglobin) is hyperbolic"
findings.note: Verbatim in the source.

findings.claim: Quoted: haemoglobin ferries oxygen "from an extreme gradient of partial pressure from lungs (where it must remain tightly bound) to tissues (where it has to be easily released)"
findings.note: Verbatim, including both parentheticals. A first fetch returned a paraphrase; a second, quote-only fetch confirmed the exact wording.

findings.claim: Myoglobin is "a storage protein sitting in muscle cytoplasm"
findings.note: The teaching article never calls myoglobin a storage protein and never says muscle: it says only "Mb, located in the cell cytoplasm, releases oxygen to the respiratory chain of the mitochondrion". The allostery review does not mention myoglobin at all. Rewritten to the source's own wording.

findings.claim: "In most vertebrates haemoglobin is a tetramer of two α-subunits and two β-subunits"
findings.note: "In most vertebrates, Hb is a tetramer, consisting of two α-subunits (α1 and α2) and two β-subunits (β1 and β2)". The "most vertebrates" qualifier is the source's own.

findings.claim: Quoted: "the tense (T) state (unliganded Hb) which exhibits low affinity for O2, and the relaxed (R) state (liganded Hb) which exhibits high affinity for O2."
findings.note: Verbatim.

findings.claim: Quoted: MWC "assumes that, upon ligand binding, the T state switches to the R state without intermediate states"
findings.note: Verbatim.

findings.claim: KNF model has one unliganded conformation changing sequentially with each binding event
findings.note: "the KNF model assumes one Hb conformation in the absence of ligand, which changes with each binding of ligand to the subunit".

findings.claim: Perutz model routes the signal through direct α1–β2 contact
findings.note: "...transmitted to other subunits through direct communication between the α1 and β2 subunits".

findings.claim: Hill coefficient 1.4 in haemoglobin Bassett against 2.6 in HbA; Bassett is a low-affinity mutant
findings.note: n = 2.6 (HbA), n = 1.4 (Hb Bassett). "Hb Bassett (αAsp94Ala) ... is characterized by a markedly reduced oxygen affinity".

findings.claim: Hill coefficient 2.6 is "below four, the number of sites"
findings.note: The source never states "four oxygen binding sites" nor relates nH to site count; it describes a tetramer with a haem pocket in each subunit. Reworded to "below four, the number of haem groups the tetramer carries", which follows directly from what the source does say.

findings.claim: P50 for normal adult human haemoglobin is "about 26 mmHg"
findings.note: "about 26 mmHg for normal adult human Hb (HbA)". Verbatim.

findings.claim: Clinical reference sources give an accepted normal P50 of 27 mmHg
findings.note: "the accepted normal P50 of 27 mmHg".

findings.claim: P50 is the oxygen tension at which haemoglobin is half saturated
findings.note: "P50 (partial pressure at which the hemoglobin molecule is half saturated with O2)".

findings.claim: Species P50: elephant 23.03 ± 0.32, human 33.02 ± 0.29, cat 43.22 ± 0.62, mouse 57.86 ± 0.76 mmHg
findings.note: All four values match Table 2 exactly.

findings.claim: Hill coefficients from 2.49 in the elephant to 3.32 in the mouse
The reanalysis "ranked mammalian haemoglobins by affinity and found it tracks body size inversely"
findings.note: BACKWARDS. The elephant (largest) has the LOWEST P50 and so the HIGHEST affinity; the mouse the reverse. Affinity rises with body size; it is P50 that falls. The source's own stated result is "an inverse linear correlation ... between the metabolic rate and Hb affinity". Rewritten to "P50 falls as body size rises", the species list reordered mouse-to-elephant, and the authors' metabolic-rate correlation quoted directly.

findings.claim: A 2019 reanalysis in eLife of classic comparative blood data
findings.note: eLife, 2019; a re-fitting of previously published Schmidt-Nielsen (1958, 1970) saturation curves, not new measurements. The provenance is now named in the body and the source note.

findings.claim: Quoted: standardised measurements "do not account for in vivo modulation of Hb-O2 affinity"
findings.note: Altered quotation. The source reads: "the P50 and Hill coefficient are commonly determined using in vitro standardized environmental conditions…which does not account for transient changes in the in vivo modulation of Hb-O2 affinity during circulatory transit". Both clauses now quoted accurately.

findings.claim: CO2 is hydrated to carbonic acid, which dissociates to bicarbonate and hydrogen ions
findings.note: "carbon dioxide is quickly converted to carbonic acid by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid immediately dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions."

findings.claim: Quoted: carbaminohaemoglobin "stabilizes the T state, lowers affinity for oxygen, and induces oxygen unloading"
findings.note: Verbatim.

findings.claim: Bohr effect: rising CO2 and falling pH lower haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
findings.note: "hemoglobin's lower affinity for oxygen secondary to increases in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide and/or decreased blood pH".

findings.claim: C-terminal αArg141 and βHis146; βHis146 salt-bridges with βAsp94 and αLys40 in deoxy Hb
findings.note: "βHis146 makes intra-subunit and inter-subunit salt-bridge interactions with βAsp94 and αLys40, while αArg141 also participates in a separate inter-subunit salt-bridge..."

findings.claim: The Bohr factor is the change in log P50 per unit change in pH
findings.note: "The Bohr factor (Φ...) was quantified by the slope of linear plots of logP50 as a function of pH (Φ = ΔlogP50/ΔpH)."

findings.claim: Bohr factor about −0.5 in human HbA under standard in vitro conditions
findings.note: "...measured under in vitro standard conditions (e.g. ~−0.5 in human HbA)". The article's "standard in vitro conditions" qualifier is the source's own.

findings.claim: Deer mouse Bohr factors −0.62 ± 0.04 (highland) and −0.57 ± 0.00 (lowland) at 37 °C
findings.note: Both match Table 2.

findings.claim: The Haldane effect "belongs to the carbon dioxide dissociation curve rather than this one"
findings.note: The source the article leaned on (NBK539815) never defines the Haldane effect — it appears there only inside a reference title. NBK526028 does define it: haemoglobin "releasing its oxygen molecules in favor of binding H+ ions", serving "as a buffering agent", with bicarbonate leaving in exchange for chloride. Re-sourced to NBK526028, rewritten to that definition, and the unsupported "belongs to the CO2 dissociation curve" assertion dropped.

findings.claim: 2,3-BPG binds the β-cleft of deoxy Hb at βHis2, βLys82, βHis143 and βHis146, stabilising the T state
findings.note: "2,3-BPG preferentially bind to the β-cleft of deoxygenated Hb making interactions with βHis2, βLys82, βHis143, and βHis146".

findings.claim: Raised 2,3-BPG shifts the curve right; raised temperature likewise
findings.note: Right-shift factors listed include "increases in temperature, 2,3-bisphosphoglyceric acid (2-3-BPG)".

findings.claim: Enthalpy of oxygenation for human HbA is −50.7 kJ per mol O2
Deer mouse haemoglobins average about −10.5 kJ per mol O2, "near enough temperature-insensitive, which matters for animals whose extremities cool"
findings.note: The −10.5 kJ/mol figure is right, but the source says "similarly low temperature sensitivities" and likens them to bovine Hb, "a known example of a temperature-insensitive Hb" — it does not call deer mouse Hb temperature-insensitive outright, and it frames the benefit conditionally: reduced sensitivity "may therefore have adaptive significance in regional heterotherms that live in polar or alpine environments". Both hedges added.

findings.claim: Fetal Hb P50 of 19 mmHg against 27 mmHg for adult haemoglobin
findings.note: "P50 for fetal Hb is 19 whereas P50 of adult Hb is 27."

findings.claim: Fetal haemoglobin α2γ2 left-shifts the curve
findings.note: "Fetal HgB (alpha2gamma2) introduces a leftward shift of the curve..."

findings.claim: The fetal left shift "is what lets oxygen move from maternal to fetal blood at all"
findings.note: Overstated and misattributed. The source credits the DOUBLE BOHR EFFECT with "facilitating oxygen transfer across the placenta from mother to fetus", and separately notes fetal Hb's higher affinity. Rewritten so the higher affinity "works alongside the double Bohr effect", with the source's phrase quoted; "at all" removed.

findings.claim: Quoted: "the high O2 tension of the lungs (100 mmHg) provides full saturation"
findings.note: Verbatim.

findings.claim: The curve plateaus at high tension and is steeper at the systemic capillaries, releasing "large amounts of oxygen"
findings.note: NBK499818: "At higher oxygen tension ... the oxygen dissociation curve plateaus. At lower oxygen tension, the slope ... is steeper." NBK539815: "large amounts of oxygen released by hemoglobin for metabolically active cells".

findings.claim: The sigmoid arises from cooperative binding
findings.note: "The sigmoid or S-shape of the curve is due to the positive cooperativity of hemoglobin."

findings.claim: Root effect: acidosis reduces not only affinity but carrying capacity
findings.note: "An acidosis not only greatly decreases Hb-O2 affinity, as in the Bohr effect, but also reduces the carrying capacity of Hb for O2".

findings.claim: Modelled arterial-to-venous pH changes of 0.2 units in trout and 0.035 units in humans; right shift increased oxygen released by 73.5 per cent in trout and 1.3 per cent in the human
findings.note: Both pH steps and both percentages confirmed against the results text.

findings.claim: The model held venous oxygen tension constant ("constant venous tension")
findings.note: The paper's stated assumption is "a constant ∆Pa-vO2" — a constant arterial-to-venous PO2 DIFFERENCE. Corrected in both places it appears (the modelling sentence and the caveat sentence), and in the source note.

findings.claim: "at half saturation, a comparable pH shift moved oxygen tension between three and twenty-one times more in the fish"
findings.note: Two errors. The paper says: "For Hb-O2 saturations up to 80% and a ΔpH close to what might be expected in vivo in trout (0.2 pH units), the ΔPO2 for rainbow trout was, at minimum, 4-fold that of the human ΔPO2 and over 21-times greater at greater ΔpH values." It is FOUR-fold, not three, and the comparison spans saturations up to 80 per cent — it is not made at half saturation. Replaced with the paper's own sentence, quoted.

findings.claim: The authors are explicit that their models hold every other part of the oxygen cascade constant, and that intracellular pH cannot be measured reliably in real time in a living animal
findings.note: "Assuming that ... all other aspects of the oxygen cascade remain constant, and in particular there is no change in tissue metabolism or perfusion"; "intracellular pH (pHi) cannot yet be reliably measured in real-time at the tissue/cellular level in vivo". Both now quoted rather than paraphrased.

findings.claim: Teleosts "spend a full pH unit" on the Root effect at the swim bladder and the eye
findings.note: Contradicted by the source. ΔpH of −0.2, −0.3, −0.55 and −1.0 were modelled, and the authors say of the last two that they "far exceed what might be seen in vivo". Replaced with "a large local acidosis" and the paper's own caveat about its larger modelled steps now stated explicitly.

findings.claim: At the swim bladder and eye, "acid-secreting cells and a countercurrent network manufacture a local acidosis on purpose"
findings.note: The word countercurrent appears nowhere in the paper, and no other cited source covers retia. The source says a "gas gland also aids in producing acid" and that the eye and swimbladder are equipped with "retia–dense capillary networks that can serve to localize and magnify an acidosis–that, in conjunction with the Root effect, greatly elevate arterial PO2". Rewritten to that wording; the /en/glossary/countercurrent-exchange link was removed with the unsupported characterisation (the glossary term itself does exist, so this was an accuracy fix, not a broken link).

findings.claim: A 2015 modelling study in PLoS One
findings.note: PLoS One. 2015 Oct 5;10(10):e0139477, Rummer & Brauner.

findings.claim: Below about 4,500 m acclimatising humans reduce Hb-O2 affinity through elevated 2,3-DPG
findings.note: "During sojourns to altitudes of ∼4500 m or less, humans demonstrate a reduced Hb-O2 affinity due to elevated production of 2,3-DPG".

findings.claim: Several species adapted to high altitude have evolved higher affinity instead
findings.note: "several animal species adapted to high-altitude environments display a higher Hb-O2 affinity compared to that of low-land counterparts".

findings.claim: Quoted: "there is ongoing debate about the advantages of higher or lower hemoglobin-oxygen (Hb-O2) affinity in humans, particularly during hypoxia"
findings.note: Verbatim. Frontiers in Physiology, review, published 14 January 2022 — the article's "2022 review in Frontiers in Physiology" is correct.

findings.claim: The benefit turns on the balance between loading in the lung and unloading in the periphery
findings.note: "homeostatic maintenance of O2 delivery and utilization during hypoxia is contingent on the balance between O2 loading in the lungs and O2 off-loading in the periphery".

findings.claim: Over 200 mutations raise affinity, defined as P50 below 24 mmHg, most falling between 12 and 17 mmHg
findings.note: "over 200 distinct mutations"; "P50 less than 24 mmHg"; "a majority of high Hb-O2 affinity hemoglobinopathies examined are associated with P50 values ranging from 12 to 17 mmHg" — "most" is a fair rendering of "a majority".

findings.claim: At Leadville, Colorado, around 3,100 m, VO2max fell about 28 and 19 per cent in two normal-affinity siblings while two high-affinity siblings showed no reduction; four siblings in all
findings.note: "Two humans with high Hb-O2 affinity and two of their siblings with normal Hb-O2 affinity were examined" at "Leadville, Colorado, ∼3100 m"; "decreased by ∼28 and 19%"; the high-affinity pair "did not demonstrate a reduction". The article's "four siblings is a case series" is accurate.

findings.claim: In normobaric hypoxia equivalent to roughly 2,600 m, high-affinity carriers lost 4 ± 5 per cent against 13 ± 6 per cent in controls
Quoted: the unloading penalty "is compensated by an associated increase in the tissue diffusion capacity of O2 (via increased muscle capillarization)"
findings.note: Verbatim from the paper's conclusion.

findings.claim: Source 1 is Subcellular Biochemistry
findings.note: Subcell Biochem 94:345–382 (2020), Ahmed, Ghatge & Safo.

findings.claim: Source 2 is a 2001 Journal of Chemical Education teaching article
findings.note: J Chem Educ, 2001, Julian Gomez-Cambronero. The article's own caveat about using it for framing rather than reference values is appropriate.

findings.claim: Source 7 is Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part A
findings.note: Comp Biochem Physiol A: Molecular & Integrative Physiology, 2016.

findings.claim: Source note 3 claims the article draws "the 240-fold carbon monoxide affinity" from NBK499818
findings.note: The source does say "CO has a 240-fold greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen", but the article body never makes any carbon monoxide claim. The source note advertised content the article does not carry, so the phrase was struck from the note. Also removed the note's "right-shift factors" attribution, which belongs to source 5.

findings.claim: ICZN Art 5: a species name "is a combination of two names (a binomen), the first being the generic name and the second being the specific name"; a subspecies takes a trinomen
findings.note: Art 5.1 and 5.2 match word for word.

findings.claim: ICN Art 23: a species name "is a binary combination consisting of the name of the genus followed by a single specific epithet"
findings.note: Art 23.1 verbatim; page confirmed as the Shenzhen Code (2018), as source 7 states.

findings.claim: Zoological nomenclature starts 1 January 1758, "the date fixed for the tenth edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae"
findings.note: Art 3.1 deems TWO works published on that date — Systema Naturae 10th ed. and Clerck's Aranei Svecici, whose names take precedence. Added Clerck.

findings.claim: No name published earlier enters the system, though earlier descriptions and illustrations may be used "as evidence"
findings.note: Art 3.2 says no name OR NOMENCLATURAL ACT enters, and that "information (such as descriptions or illustrations)" may be used — it does not say "as evidence". Wording brought to the Code's.

findings.claim: Vascular plants start 1 May 1753 with Linnaeus's Species plantarum
findings.note: Art 13.1: "1 May 1753 (Linnaeus, Species plantarum, ed. 1)" for Spermatophyta and Pteridophyta at genus rank and below.

findings.claim: Mosses start in 1801 with Hedwig
findings.note: Art 13.1 gives 1 January 1801 (Hedwig, Species muscorum frondosorum) for Musci EXCEPT Sphagnaceae. Exception added.

findings.claim: Several algal groups have later starting points still
findings.note: True (Desmidiaceae 1848, Nostocaceae heterocysteae 1886, homocysteae 1892, Oedogoniaceae 1900), but algae in general start at 1753. Replaced the vague 'algal groups' with the named Oedogoniaceae/1900 case.

findings.claim: "Every available name is attached to a name-bearing type"
findings.note: Art 61.1 reads "Each nominal taxon in the family, genus or species groups has actually or potentially a name-bearing type." The article's absolute dropped both the rank restriction and "actually or potentially". Rewritten to the Code's formulation.

findings.claim: Fixing the name-bearing type "provides the objective standard of reference for the application of the name it bears"
findings.note: Art 61.1, verbatim.

findings.claim: "no matter how the boundaries of a taxonomic taxon may vary in the opinion of zoologists the valid name of such a taxon is determined from the name-bearing type(s) considered to belong within those boundaries"
findings.note: Art 61.1.1, verbatim.

findings.claim: The type of a species-group name is a holotype, lectotype, neotype or syntypes
findings.note: Art 61.1.2: "a specimen or a set of specimens (a holotype, lectotype, neotype or syntypes)".

findings.claim: The type of a genus-group name is a nominal species; the type of a family-group name is a genus
findings.note: Art 61.1.2: "a nominal species defined objectively by its type"; "the nominal genus on which its name is based".

findings.claim: ICN: the nomenclatural type is "that element to which the name of a taxon is permanently attached" and "is not necessarily the most typical or representative element of a taxon"
findings.note: Art 7.2, both phrases verbatim.

findings.claim: Names with different types judged to belong to one taxon are subjective synonyms, revisable by a later specialist
"Names sharing a type are objective synonyms, and nothing short of Commission action can separate them"
findings.note: Art 61.1.3 allows a fixed name-bearing type to change under Arts 70.3.2 and 74-75 as well as by the Commission's plenary power, so 'nothing short of Commission action' is false. Rewritten to name the narrow Code cases alongside the plenary power.

findings.claim: The valid name is "the oldest available name applied to it, unless that name has been invalidated or another name is given precedence by any provision of the Code or by any ruling of the Commission"
findings.note: Art 23.1, verbatim including the Commission clause (confirmed on a second targeted fetch).

findings.claim: Priority "is to be used to promote stability and it is not intended to be used to upset a long-accepted name in its accustomed meaning by the introduction of a name that is its senior synonym or homonym"
findings.note: Art 23.2, verbatim.

findings.claim: The senior name must not have been used as a valid name after 1899
The junior name must appear as a presumed valid name in at least 25 works, by at least 10 authors, in the immediately preceding 50 years, spanning not less than 10 years
findings.note: Art 23.9.1.2 — all four thresholds match exactly.

findings.claim: The senior name becomes a nomen oblitum and the junior a nomen protectum
Botanical conservation "aims at retention of those names that best serve stability of nomenclature", with conserved names listed in appendices
findings.note: Art 14.2 verbatim; Art 14.1 lists App. II-IV.

findings.claim: A taxon with a given circumscription, position and rank "can bear only one correct name"

For a taxon below the rank of genus the correct name is "the combination of the final epithet of the earliest legitimate name of the taxon at the same rank, with the correct name of the genus or species to which it is assigned"
findings.note: Art 11.4, verbatim.

findings.claim: Antirrhinum spurium transferred to Linaria becomes L. spuria
findings.note: Art 11 Example 8 gives L. spuria (L.) Mill.; the full author citation is now shown, which also evidences the gender-agreement point.

findings.claim: "no proposal by the transferring author to substitute a different epithet has standing"
findings.note: Article 11 states no such rule; only Example 9 (Cassini's illegitimate renaming) bears on it obliquely. Rewritten to what 11.4 does say: the epithet is fixed as the earliest legitimate one, not chosen by the transferring author.

findings.claim: Linnaeus described the lion in Felis and the name in use is now Panthera leo (Linnaeus, 1758)
findings.note: No cited source supported this. ITIS TSN 183803 gives the accepted name Panthera leo (Linnaeus, 1758) with Felis leo Linnaeus, 1758 among its synonyms; added inline and as source 10, and ITIS added to the biology source registry. Cross-checked against GBIF, which also records Felis leo Linnaeus, 1758 as a synonym of Panthera leo.

findings.claim: MDD recorded 296 species de novo, 321 split, 357 lumped, 227 generic changes, 17 specific-epithet changes, 148 spelling changes
findings.note: All six counts match, and they are indeed MDD1 vs MDD2. The paper dates that window as August 2017-August 2024; the seven-year span is now stated, since 'comparing itself directly against its first' left the interval invisible.

findings.claim: "The 227 generic transfers altered names without altering anyone's view of which populations belong together"
findings.note: A generic transfer does change the view of which SPECIES belong together — that is what it asserts. What it leaves untouched is species delimitation. Rewritten to 'rewrote names without redrawing the boundary of a single species'.

findings.claim: Zoological authorship citation is "optional, although customary and often advisable"
findings.note: Art 51.1, verbatim.

findings.claim: The author's name follows without punctuation except in changed combinations, where it is parenthesised
findings.note: Arts 51.2 and 51.3.

findings.claim: Taenia diminuta Rudolphi becomes Hymenolepis diminuta (Rudolphi) on transfer
findings.note: Art 51.3's own worked example.

findings.claim: "The convention has a narrow exception, applied when the species-group name was originally published with a misspelling or emendation of the generic name"
findings.note: Art 51.3.1 states the exception's EFFECT — the parentheses are omitted — which the article left unsaid, so a reader could not tell which way the exception cut. Effect now stated.

findings.claim: ICN Art 49: author citation for a name with a basionym is the basionym author in parentheses followed by the author of the new combination
findings.note: Art 49.1, verbatim.

findings.claim: Medicago polymorpha var. orbicularis L., raised to species, is cited as M. orbicularis (L.) Bartal.
findings.note: Art 49 Example 1.

findings.claim: WCVP, version prepared 16 March 2021, comprised 1,190,715 records: 400,341 accepted names, 744,145 synonyms, 3,610 artificial hybrids, 42,619 unplaced names
findings.note: Quoted verbatim in the paper: "This data set, prepared on 16th Mar. 2021, comprises 1,190,715 records, including 400,341 accepted names, 744,145 synonyms, 3610 artificial hybrids and 42,619 unplaced names."

findings.claim: "Roughly two synonyms stand behind every accepted plant species name"
findings.note: The 400,341 accepted NAMES include infraspecific taxa; the same paper reports 342,953 accepted vascular plant SPECIES as of 16 April 2021. The ratio is per accepted name, not per species. Corrected, with the species figure and its date now given.

findings.claim: "Mammals, the best-catalogued class of animals"
findings.note: The paper makes no such characterisation, and no other cited source does. Superlative deleted; the sentence now just marks the ratio as steeper.

findings.claim: "50,230 curated species-rank synonyms against 6,759 valid species"
findings.note: The paper's summary sentence reads "6,759 valid mammal species ... along with nomenclatural data for 50,230 valid and synonymous species-rank scientific names" — i.e. valid names are inside the 50,230, so they are not all synonyms (the paper does contradict itself once with 'totaling 50,230 synonyms'). Restated with the unambiguous framing, and the ratio expressed as ~7.5 names per species rather than as synonyms per species.

findings.claim: 6,759 valid species: 6,629 wild extant, 113 extinct, 17 domestic
findings.note: All four figures match; 'extinct' is 'recently extinct' in the paper, now reflected.

findings.claim: Taxonomy and nomenclature are "closely allied, but separate and complementary endeavours"
findings.note: Verbatim; the full sentence continues "in developing the language of biodiversity".

findings.claim: Nomenclature "does not determine the inclusiveness or exclusiveness of any taxon, nor the rank to be accorded to any assemblage of animals, but rather provides the name that is to be used for a taxon whatever taxonomic limits and rank are given to it"
findings.note: Verbatim on the FAQ page.

findings.claim: The Commission does not patrol the literature; it rules on cases brought to it by taxonomists, acting as arbitrator
findings.note: "The ICZN does not police the use of zoological nomenclature"; "The Commission rules on Cases that are brought before it by interested parties (usually taxonomists), thus acts as an arbitrator and judge".

findings.claim: Source 7 note: the Shenzhen Code is "Superseded by the Madrid Code of 2025"
findings.note: The Madrid Code, reflecting the 2024 Madrid IBC, was published 21 July 2025 and supersedes the Shenzhen Code. The disclosure is accurate and worth keeping, since all ICN article numbers cited here are Shenzhen numbering.

findings.claim: Source 8 attribution: Scientific Data, "The World Checklist of Vascular Plants, a continuously updated resource for exploring global plant diversity"
findings.note: Govaerts, Nic Lughadha, Black, Turner & Paton (2021), Scientific Data 8:215. Source note tightened to name the 16 March 2021 dataset and the April species count now cited.

findings.claim: Source 9 attribution: Journal of Mammalogy, "How many mammal species are there now? Updates and trends in taxonomic, nomenclatural, and geographic knowledge"
findings.note: Burgin, Zijlstra, Becker et al., J. Mammalogy 106(5):1082-1117. Source note rewritten so it no longer describes the 50,230 as synonyms.

findings.claim: Quoted: coverage-based rarefaction 'encompasses changes in both components: species composition and community size'
findings.note: Misquotation. The paper's verb is 'presents', not 'encompasses': 'the coverage-based rarefaction indicator presents the changes in both components: species composition, pit's, and community size, nt'. Corrected to the source's wording, eliding the notation with an ellipsis. The paired size-based quote ('only the change in community composition') is verbatim from Corollary 1 and was left standing.

findings.claim: Over 4,800 routes across the United States, Canada and northern Mexico
findings.note: USGS says 'across the continental United States, Canada and northern Mexico'. Dropping 'continental' overstates the network's extent. Added.

findings.claim: 'Their recommendation is contested in its scope'
findings.note: No cited source supports it. The article cites only the ISME piece, which does not report itself as contested, and a targeted search for a published rebuttal or comment returned none. An unsourced 'this is disputed' hedge is a fabricated attribution to an unnamed body of critics. Clause cut; the sentence now carries only the generalisation the article actually argues.

findings.claim: 90% of known species richness reached in 1939, after 69 years of collecting and 1,309 sampled individuals
findings.note: All three numbers verbatim, but the source immediately qualifies them: 'use of a smoothed curve (MaoTau), indicates that about 50 years (but with more than 9000 individuals) should be needed to reach 90% of known richness.' The 1,309 figure is an artefact of very uneven historical effort, so quoting it alone understates the specimen effort. Added the Mao Tau caveat.

findings.claim: For the Breeding Bird Survey and freshwater fish surveys the equivalent figures were 82.6% and 82.3%
findings.note: Numbers right, phrasing invited a wrong reading. In the source, 82.6% and 82.3% are the complete and contemporary time periods respectively, pooled across BBS and FFS — not one figure per programme. Rewrote to name the two periods explicitly.

findings.claim: Quoted: Chao1 and ACE 'must not be used' with amplicon sequence variant data
findings.note: The source's sentence is scoped: 'must not be used for estimating total richness of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) datasets'. findings.claim: In the median case the actual coefficient fell below 2.5 on the coldest winter days
findings.note: Source says 'For the RC3.5 scenario, the actual COP falls below 2.5 on multiple occasions during the coldest winter days'. Two defects: 'median case' was the writer's own arithmetic on the scenario list, not the paper's label; and dropping 'on multiple occasions' turned an intermittent excursion into a standing condition. FIXED: names the rated-3.5 scenario, restores the hedge, and identifies the work as a single-city modelling study (Toulouse, France) rather than 'a recent study of air-to-air units'.

findings.claim: For a reversible heat pump the coefficient cannot exceed T_h/(T_h − T_c); 293 K against 273 K gives ~14.7
findings.sourceChecked: no cited source states it; derived from the article's own sourced bound
findings.note: The heating-COP bound was asserted as if quoted, but no cited source gives it. It is a strict consequence of 1 − T_c/T_h, which the article does establish and source, so the fix was to show the derivation rather than cut the claim. FIXED: reworded to 'the reciprocal of the engine expression: 1/(1 − T_c/T_h), which rearranges to T_h/(T_h − T_c)'. Arithmetic re-derived: 293/20 = 14.65; 3/14.65 = 20.5%, so 'roughly a fifth' holds.

findings.claim: DOE: air-source heat pumps cut electricity use by 50% vs furnaces and baseboard heaters; geothermal cuts energy use 30%–60%
findings.note: Both verbatim. The article correctly preserves DOE's own distinction — 'electricity use' for air-source, 'energy use' for ground-coupled.

findings.claim: Landsberg limit 93.3% with no irreversible entropy generation, and 85.4% for an intermediate blackbody at its optimal 2,544 K, for a 6,000 K source and 300 K ambient
findings.note: All four numbers exact, and the reversibility characterisation is right (the derivation sets S_out = S_in). But the paper's headline result is the limit on harvesting Earth's OUTGOING thermal radiation (153.1 W/m² at Ta=300 K, To=3 K); 93.3% and 85.4% are its SOLAR-illumination limits. The article's phrase 'work on harvesting from thermal radiation' attached the numbers to the wrong half of the paper. FIXED: 'radiative energy harvesting ... for solar illumination', and the Sources entry now says the limits are under solar illumination.

findings.claim: Shockley-Queisser detailed-balance limit ~34% single junction, rising to ~45% for a tandem
findings.note: Verbatim: 'can be increased from 34% for a single-junction solar cell to 45% for a tandem solar cell'.

findings.claim: Roughly 1.74 eV is the ideal top-cell bandgap over silicon
findings.note: Source states it exactly and with a condition the article dropped: 'The ideal bandgap for a series-connected tandem solar cell with Si as a bottom cell is 1.74 eV.' FIXED: removed the spurious 'roughly' and added 'series-connected', since the optimum follows from current matching in series and does not carry over unchanged to a four-terminal stack.
